text:
# Imagine Dragons: Mercury – Act 1

There have been other rock bands from Las Vegas, but none have embodied the city’s essence like [Imagine Dragons](https://pitchfork.com/artists/imagine-dragons/). Packed with all the pyrotechnics and budget-busting pageantry of the Strip, each of the band’s albums has played like an imagined Cirque Du Soleil production, as if they were designed not for stereos but for stages. If you’d never seen a picture of frontman Dan Reynolds before—and, despite this band’s monumental success, a lot of people haven’t—you might guess he looks like [Criss Angel](https://longislandweekly.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/CA-Full-Body-Studio-Black-Jacket-b.jpg).

That embrace of brute-force spectacle has made Imagine Dragons one of modern rock’s few true blockbuster attractions, one of the most streamed bands of the Spotify era. But monetizing music isn’t the same as making people care about it. With no central personality for fans to feel truly vested in, the band can seem as anonymous as the black-shirted techies that strike the Wynn Encore Theater each night. On their fifth album, _Mercury – Act 1_, Reynolds works to change that, teaming with rock’s patron saint of prestige, [Rick Rubin](https://pitchfork.com/artists/6945-rick-rubin/), for a humanizing makeover, complete with the requisite songs about suffering and mortality that Rubin demands from all of his charges.

No score yet, be the first to add.

0.0

Rubin’s presence softens Imagine Dragons’ sound in places, and after so many albums that played like the THX sound effect drawn out for an excruciating 50 minutes, that’s a welcome change of pace. In rare moments, Reynolds’ Rubin-mandated vulnerability works to his favor, especially on album highlight “Wrecked,” which he wrote about losing his sister-in-law to cancer. Here his clumsy lyricism, usually a liability, becomes an asset. When he sings, “We were there for the ups and downs/And there for the constant rounds of chemo,” it’s touching in its plainspokenness.

Overstatement is still this band’s very reason for being, though, so for most of _Mercury_ they fire their emotions out of a T-shirt cannon. Reynolds’ snarl-yell, his signature since “Radioactive,” is one of the most grating sounds in popular music, and he goes absolutely nuclear with it on “Dull Knives,” which stews in wall-punching rage even as it pleads for empathy: “I’m crying for help, it’s such a cliché/Invisible pain, it’s filling each day.” Even worse is “Cutthroat,” a fuck-shit-up, you-want-a-piece of-me Woodstock ’99 throwback that’s the most dirtbag thing [Fred Durst](https://pitchfork.com/artists/24793-fred-durst/) never wrote. Ironically, that song is immediately followed by one called “No Time for Toxic People,” a true Spider-Man-pointing-at-Spider-Man moment: If you’re looking to cut toxic people out of your life, try starting with the ones who wrote “Cutthroat.”

Elsewhere the band’s genre hopping, the secret sauce behind their billions of streams, leads to some truly stupefying combinations. With its pillow-humping synths, “Monday” is a sleazier rewrite of [Muse](https://pitchfork.com/artists/2872-muse/)’s “Madness,” while the hip-hop experiment “Follow You” sounds like [Post Malone](https://pitchfork.com/artists/33674-post-malone/) covering [Queen](https://pitchfork.com/artists/12927-queen/) at karaoke. Dopier still is the [Bleachers](https://pitchfork.com/artists/32408-bleachers/)\-styled “It’s OK,” where good intentions and implied LGBTQ allyship are undercut by goofy ’80s _Vacation_\-soundtrack vibes and the mock-Caribbean accents of its chanted chorus. Did they really intend for the album’s big self-acceptance anthem to sound this much like [Todd Rundgren](https://pitchfork.com/artists/8595-todd-rundgren/)’s “[Bang the Drum All Day](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8LdLIqkmMB0)”?

It’s truly rare to hear an album talk out of both sides of its mouth so incoherently while pandering so desperately in all directions . _Mercury_ tries to be all things to all people, but mostly it’s a headache, a grim study in just how patronizing popular music can be in 2021. Imagine Dragons do intermittently demonstrate some signs of growth, but these don’t count for much; attempts at maturity really don’t go all that far on an album that mostly sounds like a truck full of teens driving by and flashing the shocker at you.

* * *

Buy: [Rough Trade](https://cna.st/affiliate-)

_(Pitchfork earns a commission from purchases made through affiliate links on our site.)_

_Catch up every Saturday with 10 of our best-reviewed albums of the week. Sign up for the 10 to Hear newsletter_ [_here_](https://pitchfork.com/newsletter/10-to-hear)_._

_**Loom**_ is the sixth studio album by American [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") band [Imagine Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons "Imagine Dragons"), released through [Kidinakorner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidinakorner "Kidinakorner") and [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records") on June 28, 2024. The standard version comprises nine tracks, the fewest on an Imagine Dragons album to date. Produced by the band and longtime collaborators [Mattman & Robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattman_&_Robin "Mattman & Robin"), it follows their two-part studio album _[Mercury – Acts 1 & 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_–_Acts_1_&_2 "Mercury – Acts 1 & 2")_ (2022).[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1) The album marks the band's first release as a trio, due to drummer [Daniel Platzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Platzman "Daniel Platzman") announcing an indefinite hiatus from the band in March 2023, later departing from the band in August 2024.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Platzman-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

The album received generally positive reviews from music critics, and peaked at number 22 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200").

## Background and concept

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Loom_\(Imagine_Dragons_album\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and concept")\]

Every Imagine Dragons album prior to _Loom_ had followed relatively the same creative process - the band would enter the studio with 100-200 demos, and narrow it down to the final batch of songs on an album. Imagine Dragons initially followed the same process for this album, entering the studio with 150 demos written during the Mercury tour, until producers Mattman & Robin had made a suggestion to switch things up by starting over from scratch. The band proceeded to write and record 30 songs for _Loom_ over six months, the smallest amount of material Imagine Dragons had ever created for a studio album.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

The album name was inspired by the [video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loom_\(video_game\) "Loom (video game)") of the same name, with Reynolds quoting it as his introduction to music at six years old.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) A main theme of _Loom_ is "new beginnings", paralleling both Reynolds' love life of divorcing his wife and beginning to date actress [Minka Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minka_Kelly "Minka Kelly"), as well as the absence of Platzman during the album's creation.

In an interview with the _[Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press")_, lead singer [Dan Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Reynolds "Dan Reynolds") described the creative process behind the album and its cover:[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1)

> You can't really tell if it's a sunset or a sunrise, and then there are two people kind of separated standing in front of it. That really kind of sums it up thematically when I listen to it. Is the beginning of something new, or is this the end of something? And the sunset and the sunrise always kind of feels that way to me. It could be either/or.

On March 10, 2024, the band began teasing new music on their social media.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) In the following days, a [sand clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_clock "Sand clock") was displayed on the official website. By the end of March, the website started showing four doors. The four doors consisted on three different groups competing to get points on multiple mini games; the three groups were _Croyants_ (Believers), _Guerriers_ (Warriors) and _Rêveurs_ (Dreamers), divided according to previous music preference of the users. Each of these groups were referencing a song from the band: "[Believer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Believer_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Believer (Imagine Dragons song)")", "[Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warriors_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Warriors (Imagine Dragons song)")" and "Dream".[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

Each week, a new door was revealed, showing a new game and some clues about the release date or some of the new songs' lyrics. On April 1, with the opening of the second door, they announced a new song titled "[Eyes Closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_Closed_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Eyes Closed (Imagine Dragons song)")" would be released on April 3.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-eyesClosed-9) On April 22, after all four doors were opened, a fifth door –referencing the "Eyes Closed" music video– was revealed, which finally confirmed the new album's name to be _LOOM_.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1) Additionally, a new [world tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loom_World_Tour "Loom World Tour") was announced to begin during the summer.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

For the winning team of the four doors, the _Croyants_, a video was shared with snippets for three songs from the new album, titled: "Fire in These Hills", "[Nice to Meet You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Nice to Meet You (Imagine Dragons song)")" and "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Wake Up (Imagine Dragons song)")".[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

On April 25, a post on social media from the band's official accounts teased a new collaboration.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) On April 30, their official account announced a new version of "Eyes Closed" featuring Colombian singer [J Balvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J_Balvin "J Balvin"). It was released on May 3.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

The official track list, along with the song lengths, were unveiled on May 8.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

A second single "[Nice to Meet You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Nice to Meet You (Imagine Dragons song)")" was released on May 24.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

The band released a music video for "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Wake Up (Imagine Dragons song)")" on July 2.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

A remix of "[Take Me to the Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_to_the_Beach "Take Me to the Beach")" featuring [Baker Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_Boy "Baker Boy") was released on October 11.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Another featuring [Ernia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernia "Ernia") was released on October 18.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) A third remix with [Jungeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungeli "Jungeli") was released on November 1,[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) followed by a fourth with [Ado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ado_\(singer\) "Ado (singer)") on December 16.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

_Loom_ received generally positive reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism"). At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an [average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_mean "Weighted mean") score of 67, based on 4 reviews, which indicates "generally favorable reviews". This is the first time one of the band's albums received a positive score.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-21)

Neil Z. Yeung of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") gave the album a positive review, stating "longtime fans of their aggressive empowerment anthems will delight in this pseudo-'return to form' from the Vegas quartet" and described it as "one of their most satisfying and immediate sets to date".[\[22\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-22) Jon Dolan of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ said that the album "finds the band piloting some musical and personal transitions" and later concluding that "Such kind-vibes moments show that within the vast spaces these guys work in, there's always room for growth".[\[26\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-26) Tom Carr of _[The Arts Desk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_Desk "The Arts Desk")_ remarked that "\[_LOOM_\] may not be challenging to listen to, but it can't be denied that Imagine Dragons have a knack for bringing together various textures, and condensing them into something that goes down smooth" and said that "Overall, _LOOM_ pleases without blazing any new trails".[\[23\]](#cite_note-ArtsDesk-23) Robin Murray of _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_ gave the album a mixed review, summarizing that it was a "succinct if somewhat unfulfilling return".[\[24\]](#cite_note-Clash-24)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Loom_\(Imagine_Dragons_album\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

_Loom_ debuted at number 22 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") with 28,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] It is the band's first album to not peak in the top ten of the chart, as well as their first to not have a song chart on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").

All tracks are written by [Dan Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Reynolds "Dan Reynolds"), [Wayne Sermon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Sermon "Wayne Sermon"), [Ben McKee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_McKee "Ben McKee"), [Mattias Larsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattias_Larsson "Mattias Larsson"), and [Robin Fredriksson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Fredriksson "Robin Fredriksson"), except where noted.

_**Loom**_ is the sixth studio album by American [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") band [Imagine Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons "Imagine Dragons"), released through [Kidinakorner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidinakorner "Kidinakorner") and [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records") on June 28, 2024. The standard version comprises nine tracks, the fewest on an Imagine Dragons album to date. Produced by the band and longtime collaborators [Mattman & Robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattman_&_Robin "Mattman & Robin"), it follows their two-part studio album _[Mercury – Acts 1 & 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_–_Acts_1_&_2 "Mercury – Acts 1 & 2")_ (2022).[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1) The album marks the band's first release as a trio, due to drummer [Daniel Platzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Platzman "Daniel Platzman") announcing an indefinite hiatus from the band in March 2023, later departing from the band in August 2024.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Platzman-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

The album received generally positive reviews from music critics, and peaked at number 22 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200").

## Background and concept

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Loom_\(Imagine_Dragons_album\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and concept")\]

Every Imagine Dragons album prior to _Loom_ had followed relatively the same creative process - the band would enter the studio with 100-200 demos, and narrow it down to the final batch of songs on an album. Imagine Dragons initially followed the same process for this album, entering the studio with 150 demos written during the Mercury tour, until producers Mattman & Robin had made a suggestion to switch things up by starting over from scratch. The band proceeded to write and record 30 songs for _Loom_ over six months, the smallest amount of material Imagine Dragons had ever created for a studio album.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

The album name was inspired by the [video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loom_\(video_game\) "Loom (video game)") of the same name, with Reynolds quoting it as his introduction to music at six years old.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) A main theme of _Loom_ is "new beginnings", paralleling both Reynolds' love life of divorcing his wife and beginning to date actress [Minka Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minka_Kelly "Minka Kelly"), as well as the absence of Platzman during the album's creation.

In an interview with the _[Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press")_, lead singer [Dan Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Reynolds "Dan Reynolds") described the creative process behind the album and its cover:[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1)

> You can't really tell if it's a sunset or a sunrise, and then there are two people kind of separated standing in front of it. That really kind of sums it up thematically when I listen to it. Is the beginning of something new, or is this the end of something? And the sunset and the sunrise always kind of feels that way to me. It could be either/or.

On March 10, 2024, the band began teasing new music on their social media.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) In the following days, a [sand clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_clock "Sand clock") was displayed on the official website. By the end of March, the website started showing four doors. The four doors consisted on three different groups competing to get points on multiple mini games; the three groups were _Croyants_ (Believers), _Guerriers_ (Warriors) and _Rêveurs_ (Dreamers), divided according to previous music preference of the users. Each of these groups were referencing a song from the band: "[Believer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Believer_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Believer (Imagine Dragons song)")", "[Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warriors_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Warriors (Imagine Dragons song)")" and "Dream".[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)

Each week, a new door was revealed, showing a new game and some clues about the release date or some of the new songs' lyrics. On April 1, with the opening of the second door, they announced a new song titled "[Eyes Closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_Closed_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Eyes Closed (Imagine Dragons song)")" would be released on April 3.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-eyesClosed-9) On April 22, after all four doors were opened, a fifth door –referencing the "Eyes Closed" music video– was revealed, which finally confirmed the new album's name to be _LOOM_.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Heavy_concepts-1) Additionally, a new [world tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loom_World_Tour "Loom World Tour") was announced to begin during the summer.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

For the winning team of the four doors, the _Croyants_, a video was shared with snippets for three songs from the new album, titled: "Fire in These Hills", "[Nice to Meet You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Nice to Meet You (Imagine Dragons song)")" and "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Wake Up (Imagine Dragons song)")".[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

On April 25, a post on social media from the band's official accounts teased a new collaboration.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) On April 30, their official account announced a new version of "Eyes Closed" featuring Colombian singer [J Balvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J_Balvin "J Balvin"). It was released on May 3.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

The official track list, along with the song lengths, were unveiled on May 8.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

A second single "[Nice to Meet You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Nice to Meet You (Imagine Dragons song)")" was released on May 24.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

The band released a music video for "[Wake Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Up_\(Imagine_Dragons_song\) "Wake Up (Imagine Dragons song)")" on July 2.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

A remix of "[Take Me to the Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_to_the_Beach "Take Me to the Beach")" featuring [Baker Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_Boy "Baker Boy") was released on October 11.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Another featuring [Ernia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernia "Ernia") was released on October 18.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) A third remix with [Jungeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungeli "Jungeli") was released on November 1,[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) followed by a fourth with [Ado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ado_\(singer\) "Ado (singer)") on December 16.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

_Loom_ received generally positive reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism"). At [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an [average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_mean "Weighted mean") score of 67, based on 4 reviews, which indicates "generally favorable reviews". This is the first time one of the band's albums received a positive score.[\[21\]](#cite_note-Metacritic-21)

Neil Z. Yeung of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") gave the album a positive review, stating "longtime fans of their aggressive empowerment anthems will delight in this pseudo-'return to form' from the Vegas quartet" and described it as "one of their most satisfying and immediate sets to date".[\[22\]](#cite_note-AllMusic-22) Jon Dolan of _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ said that the album "finds the band piloting some musical and personal transitions" and later concluding that "Such kind-vibes moments show that within the vast spaces these guys work in, there's always room for growth".[\[26\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-26) Tom Carr of _[The Arts Desk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Arts_Desk "The Arts Desk")_ remarked that "\[_LOOM_\] may not be challenging to listen to, but it can't be denied that Imagine Dragons have a knack for bringing together various textures, and condensing them into something that goes down smooth" and said that "Overall, _LOOM_ pleases without blazing any new trails".[\[23\]](#cite_note-ArtsDesk-23) Robin Murray of _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash_\(magazine\) "Clash (magazine)")_ gave the album a mixed review, summarizing that it was a "succinct if somewhat unfulfilling return".[\[24\]](#cite_note-Clash-24)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Loom_\(Imagine_Dragons_album\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

_Loom_ debuted at number 22 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") with 28,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] It is the band's first album to not peak in the top ten of the chart, as well as their first to not have a song chart on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").

All tracks are written by [Dan Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Reynolds "Dan Reynolds"), [Wayne Sermon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Sermon "Wayne Sermon"), [Ben McKee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_McKee "Ben McKee"), [Mattias Larsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattias_Larsson "Mattias Larsson"), and [Robin Fredriksson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Fredriksson "Robin Fredriksson"), except where noted.

text:
# Inside Imagine Dragons’ ‘Loom’: Dan Reynolds On How A Sense Of Foreboding Led To The Band’s Most Colorful Album | Grammy

For a dozen years now, [Imagine Dragons](https://www.grammy.com/artists/imagine-dragons/18215/) have delivered melodic anthems that have resonated with audiences from Idaho to Italy. Whether you call the band’s sound arena rock, power pop or formulaic does not matter. What _does_ is the effect these soundscapes have on the masses, album after album.

The Las Vegas trio of [Dan Reynolds,](https://www.grammy.com/artists/dan-reynolds/18072/) [Ben McKee](https://www.grammy.com/artists/ben-mckee/17998/) and [Wayne Sermon](https://www.grammy.com/artists/wayne-sermon/18115/) may divide critics and peers, but there is no denying they are master craftsmen of earworms. The GRAMMY-winning group has served hit after Billboard-topping hit, [racking up](https://www.universalmusic.ca/press-releases/imagine-dragons-to-unveil-new-album-loom-on-june-28th-and-launch-north-american-headline-tour/) sales of 74 million album equivalents, 65 million digital songs and over 160 billion streams.

Frontman and chief lyricist Reynolds despises labels and says conversations about genre are "trite." And, anyway, the songwriter does not make music with fans or critics in mind. Instead, it’s about what he's feeling at any given moment and whether the melody moves him.

"I love things that are melodic," Reynolds tells GRAMMY.com. "I was a classical pianist for 10 years from six to 16 — playing Chopin, Beethoven and Bach — and their songs feature pleasing melodies and intervals. My brain was formed in that classical piano training and that’s still where I write melodies from."

On their sixth studio album, _Loom_, Imagine Dragons continue the upward trajectory that started with their GRAMMY-winning debut _Night Visions_. _Loom_ features nine new songs marked by big choruses, pleasing melodies and lyrics that concurrently make you cringe at the clichés and sing along.

Following a period of heavy loss for Reynolds when his grief hung like an invisible cobweb clouding his thoughts — and that _Mercury - Acts 1 & 2_ chronicled in song— Imagine Dragons went their separate ways. A break was needed and family time called before any thoughts were given to what loomed next.

**Learn more:** [Inside Imagine Dragons' Biggest Hits: Dan Reynolds Details How "Believer," "Radioactive" & More Came To Be](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)

_Loom_ is definitely a more joyful record, but buried beneath these sanguine melodies there is still some sadness. In between recording the last album and this one, Reynolds went through a divorce — a life change that is explored in songs like "Don’t Forget Me" and "Fire in These Hills."

For Reynolds, playing live to sold-out arenas and seeing thousands of strangers singing — just like writing songs — is therapeutic. Sporting a plain white t-shirt, with a rack of guitars behind him, the singer-songwriter discussed navigating change, catharsis, the inspirations behind _Loom_, and why he makes music today is no different than what led him to penning his first-ever song.

"I’m in therapy every week and I have been since I was young," says Reynolds, adding that he started writing music at age 12 to handle emotional distress. "I didn’t know how to say what I was feeling and it wasn’t working by just writing it in a journal. Something about singing those words and putting it over a sonic soundscape felt cathartic. This record was no different and it felt really good."

Ahead of _Loom’s_ release on June 28, GRAMMY.com chatted with Reynolds via Zoom about the inspirsations behind what he considers the band’s most colorful record. The 36-year-old melody maker appeared affable, admitted to currently being sober, and that he was excited to hit the road again with his bandmates for a 30-plus date North American tour that begins at the end of July.

## A Sense Of Foreboding, Good And Bad

Multiple members of Imagine Dragons threw out names for their new record, Reynolds notes. "'Loom' just came to me out of nowhere during the filming of our first video. I was like, 'Guys, what do you think?' Within minutes they all loved it."

Reynolds likes the ideas and connotations that come with such a simple word: that something is coming. "The word feels ominous, but it can also be positive," he explains. "This record really dives into change as a lot of change was happening in my life when I wrote these songs."

Beyond those looming feelings, good and bad, Reynolds says he also loved "loom" as a noun. "It’s a very colorful record and a loom brings to mind the intertwining of different colors."

## Mattman & Robin

After working with [Rick Rubin](https://www.grammy.com/artists/rick-rubin/13812/) and having several "cooks in the kitchen" on the last record, Swedish duo Mattman and Robin (Mattias Per Larsson and Robin Lennart Fredriksson) were the sole studio chefs spearheading this production. The difference is reflected in _Loom_'s finished sound.

"This record is solely Mattman & Robin and because of that it’s our most cohesive, concise and pointed record," Reynolds says. "For our own sanity, this time we wanted to make a record that told a very specific story and that sounded like a specific color. I believe we accomplished that better than ever before because we worked with only one producer."

## Starting From Square One

The creation of the Imagine Dragons’ sixth album also differed from all their previous projects when it came to the artistic approach and the song-selection process. "For every other record, I arrived at the studio with 150 or more demos that I had put down over a two-year period," Reynolds recalls, adding that the group brought in about 200 demos, selected 70, and recorded 50 during their sessions with Rick Rubin.

While Reynolds had about 150 demos this time around, Mattman and Robin suggested that they "wipe the slate clean, throw out all these demos, and start from square one." Reynolds loved the idea, "because I love to write and I’m always writing."

He wrote about 30 new songs in the studio over four to six months, and then narrowed those down. "It was all very collaborative."

## Feeling Colors

Reflecting about the completed record, Reynolds admits that _Loom_ feels like the most up-tempo, concise body of work Imagine Dragons’ has ever done; it’s also the most colorful.

"That’s the reason we chose the sunset/sunrise artwork for the cover because the image can be perceived either way," Reynolds explains. "The record feels like the beginning of things and also the death of things … It's all about change. There are definitely more bright songs than any other record we’ve done, but there are also moments of reflection and heartache."

Reynolds is not one to keep a diary or write notes on his phone. Music is his journal.

"I’ve never been a person to write down an idea and then work on that idea," the songwriter explains. "I always write the same way: I sit down at a piano, with a guitar or at a computer with no theme in mind and create a soundscape that is an honest output of whatever I’m feeling. I then write lyrics and melody to that feeling. It’s been that same way since I was 12 and started writing songs … What I’m feeling in the moment is usually what it’s going to be."

## The Beauty & Safety Of Metaphor

Ever since Reynolds started processing his emotions through music and penned his first song as a pre-teen, he hid behind metaphors — afraid to speak his truth. During these formative years, this truth-telling usually centered on his religious beliefs. Reynolds was raised, along with his nine siblings, as a follower of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Reynolds admits that he relied too heavily on figures of speech as a writer, especially when it came to describing his relationship with Mormonism. 

Today, the artist no longer hides behind his words. "When I started writing, I was fearful of the people I love understanding what I was saying," Reynolds explains. "I was not thinking back then about the common listener; the only ones who heard my music, from the time I was 12 to 14, were my parents and I sure as hell did not want my mom to hear a song and think, ‘Are you doubting Joseph Smith!’" 

Reynolds leaned into metaphor. "so my mom would not know what I was talking about" — and that trajectory continued into his writing style on the first few Imagine Dragons records. 

"When I listen to _Night Visions_, it’s very metaphorical," Reynolds reflects. "'Radioactive' is a song about depression; yet, most people hear it and think it’s a song about the apocalypse!" 

However, some of Reynolds’ favorite songwriters — [Paul Simon](https://www.grammy.com/artists/paul-simon/6579/), [Billy Joel](https://www.grammy.com/artists/billy-joel/12071/), [Bob Dylan](https://www.grammy.com/artists/bob-dylan/3014/) and [Cat Stevens](https://www.grammy.com/artists/yusuf-cat-stevens/188936/) — are not overly metaphorical. Working with Rick Rubin on the previous Imagine Dragons double record really helped the songwriter reduce his reliance on imagery and be more authentic. "Rick was always telling me to peel back a little bit, become more vulnerable and stop being such a scaredy-cat," he says. 

Metaphors and deeper meanings aside, Reynolds stresses that while he tries to add some lyricism to his words. What matters most, he notes, is that he sings his truth and it’s believable.  

## Ch-Ch-Ch-Changes

Change is a constant in life and that theme weaves throughout _Loom_. Like French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr wrote in 1894, "_plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose._" This  aphorism, loosely translated, means the more things change, the more they stay the same.  

"There are some things in my life that never change and I’ve accepted that," Reynolds says. "One of them is that mental health has always been a bit of a struggle for me, but music helps a lot. At the same time, other things do change. I’m 36 now and I’m not the same person I was when we put out our first record and I was 22." 

The throughline in Imagine Dragons' sound is "the human experience told from a self-reflective narrative view," Reynolds continues, adding that _Loom_ felt cathartic. 

## False Empowerment

_Loom’s_ first single, "Eyes Closed," arrived May 3. The genre-bending song fuses rap, rock and pop, to create another Imagine Dragons anthem. 

"'Eyes Closed' is about something that looks perfect and idyllic and then you tap it and it falls into a million pieces," Reynolds explains. "The idea behind that song is that I could do this with my eyes closed, it’s so easy, but the reality is I was not really loving myself or feeling any of those things I was writing about."

It's a theme Reynolds revisits often. "I write a lot of songs because I’m in a bad place and I’m trying to bring about a false sense of confidence, security and empowerment," he says. "I meet people and they say, ‘I work out to this song every morning and it gets my day going,’ and I reply, ‘I’m glad because I really wasn’t going that day!’"

## Their International Fanbase 

_Loom_ closes with a reprise of "Eyes Closed" featuring Colombian reggaeton maestro [J. Balvin](https://www.grammy.com/artists/j-balvin/243132/). Imagine Dragons are no strangers to collabs. In the past, the band have recorded features with the likes of [Kendrick Lamar](https://www.grammy.com/artists/kendrick-lamar/17949/), [Lil Wayne](https://www.grammy.com/artists/lil-wayne/4037/) and [Wiz Khalifa](https://www.grammy.com/artists/cameron-thomaz/10512/), but as Reynolds explains, they are always selective in choosing these collaborations. "We don’t collaborate a lot because personally I hate it when the artists I love collaborate too much. I’m like, _I want to listen to you … I was waiting for a record from you._

"'Eyes Closed' really felt like the second verse could go in a different direction," Reynolds notes. "I had been listening to something from J. Balvin and I said to the band, ‘This could be cool and interesting, why don’t we try it?’ I’m really happy with how it turned out."

Reynolds adds that Imagine Dragons has become more of an international group that's bigger outside of its home nation. Touring globally has been a boon for the band: "We’ve enjoyed seeing and experiencing different cultures and witnessing how music bypasses all cultures," Reynolds says. "We go places where English is not the first language and people still seem to understand everything we are saying because they just feel it."

## Reynold's Faith

As Reynolds’s conversation with GRAMMY.com comes to a close, the songwriter is asked about the inspiration behind the sixth song on Loom: "God’s Don’t Pray."

"It wouldn’t be an Imagine Dragons record without me alluding to my faith," he says. "I’m not a religious person anymore, but as anyone who grows up in religion knows — especially when the rest of your family still follows that faith — it’s still such a prevalent part of your life that it is impossible to write a record without delving into religiosity and the lack thereof."

# Inside Imagine Dragons’ ‘Loom’: Dan Reynolds On How A Sense Of Foreboding Led To The Band’s Most Colorful Album | Grammy

For a dozen years now, [Imagine Dragons](https://www.grammy.com/artists/imagine-dragons/18215/) have delivered melodic anthems that have resonated with audiences from Idaho to Italy. Whether you call the band’s sound arena rock, power pop or formulaic does not matter. What _does_ is the effect these soundscapes have on the masses, album after album.

The Las Vegas trio of [Dan Reynolds,](https://www.grammy.com/artists/dan-reynolds/18072/) [Ben McKee](https://www.grammy.com/artists/ben-mckee/17998/) and [Wayne Sermon](https://www.grammy.com/artists/wayne-sermon/18115/) may divide critics and peers, but there is no denying they are master craftsmen of earworms. The GRAMMY-winning group has served hit after Billboard-topping hit, [racking up](https://www.universalmusic.ca/press-releases/imagine-dragons-to-unveil-new-album-loom-on-june-28th-and-launch-north-american-headline-tour/) sales of 74 million album equivalents, 65 million digital songs and over 160 billion streams.

Frontman and chief lyricist Reynolds despises labels and says conversations about genre are "trite." And, anyway, the songwriter does not make music with fans or critics in mind. Instead, it’s about what he's feeling at any given moment and whether the melody moves him.

"I love things that are melodic," Reynolds tells GRAMMY.com. "I was a classical pianist for 10 years from six to 16 — playing Chopin, Beethoven and Bach — and their songs feature pleasing melodies and intervals. My brain was formed in that classical piano training and that’s still where I write melodies from."

On their sixth studio album, _Loom_, Imagine Dragons continue the upward trajectory that started with their GRAMMY-winning debut _Night Visions_. _Loom_ features nine new songs marked by big choruses, pleasing melodies and lyrics that concurrently make you cringe at the clichés and sing along.

Following a period of heavy loss for Reynolds when his grief hung like an invisible cobweb clouding his thoughts — and that _Mercury - Acts 1 & 2_ chronicled in song— Imagine Dragons went their separate ways. A break was needed and family time called before any thoughts were given to what loomed next.

**Learn more:** [Inside Imagine Dragons' Biggest Hits: Dan Reynolds Details How "Believer," "Radioactive" & More Came To Be](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)

_Loom_ is definitely a more joyful record, but buried beneath these sanguine melodies there is still some sadness. In between recording the last album and this one, Reynolds went through a divorce — a life change that is explored in songs like "Don’t Forget Me" and "Fire in These Hills."

For Reynolds, playing live to sold-out arenas and seeing thousands of strangers singing — just like writing songs — is therapeutic. Sporting a plain white t-shirt, with a rack of guitars behind him, the singer-songwriter discussed navigating change, catharsis, the inspirations behind _Loom_, and why he makes music today is no different than what led him to penning his first-ever song.

"I’m in therapy every week and I have been since I was young," says Reynolds, adding that he started writing music at age 12 to handle emotional distress. "I didn’t know how to say what I was feeling and it wasn’t working by just writing it in a journal. Something about singing those words and putting it over a sonic soundscape felt cathartic. This record was no different and it felt really good."

Ahead of _Loom’s_ release on June 28, GRAMMY.com chatted with Reynolds via Zoom about the inspirsations behind what he considers the band’s most colorful record. The 36-year-old melody maker appeared affable, admitted to currently being sober, and that he was excited to hit the road again with his bandmates for a 30-plus date North American tour that begins at the end of July.

## A Sense Of Foreboding, Good And Bad

Multiple members of Imagine Dragons threw out names for their new record, Reynolds notes. "'Loom' just came to me out of nowhere during the filming of our first video. I was like, 'Guys, what do you think?' Within minutes they all loved it."

Reynolds likes the ideas and connotations that come with such a simple word: that something is coming. "The word feels ominous, but it can also be positive," he explains. "This record really dives into change as a lot of change was happening in my life when I wrote these songs."

Beyond those looming feelings, good and bad, Reynolds says he also loved "loom" as a noun. "It’s a very colorful record and a loom brings to mind the intertwining of different colors."

## Mattman & Robin

After working with [Rick Rubin](https://www.grammy.com/artists/rick-rubin/13812/) and having several "cooks in the kitchen" on the last record, Swedish duo Mattman and Robin (Mattias Per Larsson and Robin Lennart Fredriksson) were the sole studio chefs spearheading this production. The difference is reflected in _Loom_'s finished sound.

"This record is solely Mattman & Robin and because of that it’s our most cohesive, concise and pointed record," Reynolds says. "For our own sanity, this time we wanted to make a record that told a very specific story and that sounded like a specific color. I believe we accomplished that better than ever before because we worked with only one producer."

## Starting From Square One

The creation of the Imagine Dragons’ sixth album also differed from all their previous projects when it came to the artistic approach and the song-selection process. "For every other record, I arrived at the studio with 150 or more demos that I had put down over a two-year period," Reynolds recalls, adding that the group brought in about 200 demos, selected 70, and recorded 50 during their sessions with Rick Rubin.

While Reynolds had about 150 demos this time around, Mattman and Robin suggested that they "wipe the slate clean, throw out all these demos, and start from square one." Reynolds loved the idea, "because I love to write and I’m always writing."

He wrote about 30 new songs in the studio over four to six months, and then narrowed those down. "It was all very collaborative."

## Feeling Colors

Reflecting about the completed record, Reynolds admits that _Loom_ feels like the most up-tempo, concise body of work Imagine Dragons’ has ever done; it’s also the most colorful.

"That’s the reason we chose the sunset/sunrise artwork for the cover because the image can be perceived either way," Reynolds explains. "The record feels like the beginning of things and also the death of things … It's all about change. There are definitely more bright songs than any other record we’ve done, but there are also moments of reflection and heartache."

Reynolds is not one to keep a diary or write notes on his phone. Music is his journal.

"I’ve never been a person to write down an idea and then work on that idea," the songwriter explains. "I always write the same way: I sit down at a piano, with a guitar or at a computer with no theme in mind and create a soundscape that is an honest output of whatever I’m feeling. I then write lyrics and melody to that feeling. It’s been that same way since I was 12 and started writing songs … What I’m feeling in the moment is usually what it’s going to be."

## The Beauty & Safety Of Metaphor

Ever since Reynolds started processing his emotions through music and penned his first song as a pre-teen, he hid behind metaphors — afraid to speak his truth. During these formative years, this truth-telling usually centered on his religious beliefs. Reynolds was raised, along with his nine siblings, as a follower of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Reynolds admits that he relied too heavily on figures of speech as a writer, especially when it came to describing his relationship with Mormonism. 

Today, the artist no longer hides behind his words. "When I started writing, I was fearful of the people I love understanding what I was saying," Reynolds explains. "I was not thinking back then about the common listener; the only ones who heard my music, from the time I was 12 to 14, were my parents and I sure as hell did not want my mom to hear a song and think, ‘Are you doubting Joseph Smith!’" 

Reynolds leaned into metaphor. "so my mom would not know what I was talking about" — and that trajectory continued into his writing style on the first few Imagine Dragons records. 

"When I listen to _Night Visions_, it’s very metaphorical," Reynolds reflects. "'Radioactive' is a song about depression; yet, most people hear it and think it’s a song about the apocalypse!" 

However, some of Reynolds’ favorite songwriters — [Paul Simon](https://www.grammy.com/artists/paul-simon/6579/), [Billy Joel](https://www.grammy.com/artists/billy-joel/12071/), [Bob Dylan](https://www.grammy.com/artists/bob-dylan/3014/) and [Cat Stevens](https://www.grammy.com/artists/yusuf-cat-stevens/188936/) — are not overly metaphorical. Working with Rick Rubin on the previous Imagine Dragons double record really helped the songwriter reduce his reliance on imagery and be more authentic. "Rick was always telling me to peel back a little bit, become more vulnerable and stop being such a scaredy-cat," he says. 

Metaphors and deeper meanings aside, Reynolds stresses that while he tries to add some lyricism to his words. What matters most, he notes, is that he sings his truth and it’s believable.  

## Ch-Ch-Ch-Changes

Change is a constant in life and that theme weaves throughout _Loom_. Like French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr wrote in 1894, "_plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose._" This  aphorism, loosely translated, means the more things change, the more they stay the same.  

"There are some things in my life that never change and I’ve accepted that," Reynolds says. "One of them is that mental health has always been a bit of a struggle for me, but music helps a lot. At the same time, other things do change. I’m 36 now and I’m not the same person I was when we put out our first record and I was 22." 

The throughline in Imagine Dragons' sound is "the human experience told from a self-reflective narrative view," Reynolds continues, adding that _Loom_ felt cathartic. 

## False Empowerment

_Loom’s_ first single, "Eyes Closed," arrived May 3. The genre-bending song fuses rap, rock and pop, to create another Imagine Dragons anthem. 

"'Eyes Closed' is about something that looks perfect and idyllic and then you tap it and it falls into a million pieces," Reynolds explains. "The idea behind that song is that I could do this with my eyes closed, it’s so easy, but the reality is I was not really loving myself or feeling any of those things I was writing about."

It's a theme Reynolds revisits often. "I write a lot of songs because I’m in a bad place and I’m trying to bring about a false sense of confidence, security and empowerment," he says. "I meet people and they say, ‘I work out to this song every morning and it gets my day going,’ and I reply, ‘I’m glad because I really wasn’t going that day!’"

## Their International Fanbase 

_Loom_ closes with a reprise of "Eyes Closed" featuring Colombian reggaeton maestro [J. Balvin](https://www.grammy.com/artists/j-balvin/243132/). Imagine Dragons are no strangers to collabs. In the past, the band have recorded features with the likes of [Kendrick Lamar](https://www.grammy.com/artists/kendrick-lamar/17949/), [Lil Wayne](https://www.grammy.com/artists/lil-wayne/4037/) and [Wiz Khalifa](https://www.grammy.com/artists/cameron-thomaz/10512/), but as Reynolds explains, they are always selective in choosing these collaborations. "We don’t collaborate a lot because personally I hate it when the artists I love collaborate too much. I’m like, _I want to listen to you … I was waiting for a record from you._

"'Eyes Closed' really felt like the second verse could go in a different direction," Reynolds notes. "I had been listening to something from J. Balvin and I said to the band, ‘This could be cool and interesting, why don’t we try it?’ I’m really happy with how it turned out."

Reynolds adds that Imagine Dragons has become more of an international group that's bigger outside of its home nation. Touring globally has been a boon for the band: "We’ve enjoyed seeing and experiencing different cultures and witnessing how music bypasses all cultures," Reynolds says. "We go places where English is not the first language and people still seem to understand everything we are saying because they just feel it."

## Reynold's Faith

As Reynolds’s conversation with GRAMMY.com comes to a close, the songwriter is asked about the inspiration behind the sixth song on Loom: "God’s Don’t Pray."

"It wouldn’t be an Imagine Dragons record without me alluding to my faith," he says. "I’m not a religious person anymore, but as anyone who grows up in religion knows — especially when the rest of your family still follows that faith — it’s still such a prevalent part of your life that it is impossible to write a record without delving into religiosity and the lack thereof."

In the grand scheme of things, [Imagine Dragons](https://www.loudersound.com/features/who-the-f-k-are-imagine-dragons) are indubitably massive, boasting squillions of streams and downloads. The Las Vegas quartet have won mega industry awards, filled stadiums and headlined stages at last year’s Reading and Leeds festivals. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned them in dispatches. 

With _Loom_, their sixth album, we’re told that “stylistic boundaries have disappeared entirely”. 

Trouble is, the rock component seems to have vanished. 

The single _Eyes Closed_ features reggaeton artist J Balvin, which gives you some idea where this is headed. One track, the bass-heavy _Kid_, stands out above the formulaic pummelling of percussion pads. The majority is syncopated lightweight pop, as if selected by algorithms for mass consumption.

# Research: Imagine Dragons — the "rock songs that chart every time" lane (Dan Reynolds + Alex da Kid + Mattman & Robin)

## Summary
Imagine Dragons are the last rock act with mainstream Hot 100 muscle: five top-10s ("Radioactive" #2, "Demons" #6, "Believer" #4, "Thunder" #4, "Enemy" #5), the only group in RIAA history with four Diamond-plus singles, and "Radioactive"'s record 87-week Hot 100 run. The repeatable machine is documented in their own words: Dan Reynolds writes alone from a melodic germ and a "false empowerment" lyric — single-word refrains over universal pain/struggle vocabulary — and producer teams (Alex da Kid's beat-first sessions, then the Swedish minimalists Mattman & Robin) build the trademark verse→pre-chorus-lift→explosive-drop hook, engineered for radio and sync. The press critique is equally documented: Pitchfork ("machine learning output"), Spin ("algorithmic playlists"), and Classic Rock ("as if selected by algorithms") all call the formula obvious — yet Billboard staff concede "they've mastered the formula for a hit."

---

## 1) Verified credentials & 2020–2025 relevance (Billboard facts)

**Career base (verified):**
- Five Hot 100 top 10s: "Radioactive" (#2, 2013, 87 weeks on the Hot 100 — the longest run in chart history until The Weeknd's "Blinding Lights" broke it in 2021), "Demons" (#6), "Believer" (#4, 2017), "Thunder" (#4, 2017), "Enemy" (#5, 2022). Plus top-20s "It's Time" (#15), "Whatever It Takes" (#12), "Sucker for Pain" (top 20), "Natural" (#13). [Billboard Five Burning Questions](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-five-burning-questions-1235050926/); [Wikipedia (Rolling Stone/Billboard citations)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons)
- Billboard's own framing: "'Enemy' marks the fifth top 10 hit for Imagine Dragons in their decade-plus career — basically an unmatched level of crossover success for any kind of band that's emerged in the last 10 years." [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-five-burning-questions-1235050926/)
- RIAA: the only group with **four** songs certified higher than Diamond ("Radioactive," "Demons," "Believer," "Thunder"); "Believer" was the first ID song past 2B Spotify streams and 2B YouTube views. [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons)
- "Believer" spent 29 weeks at #1 on Billboard's Hot Rock & Alternative Songs (their longest run on that tally). [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)
- 74M albums + 65M digital songs sold; 160B career streams. [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing)

**2020–2025 specifics:**
- **"Enemy" (w/ JID)** — released Oct 28, 2021 as the *Arcane* theme; debuted #85 (Dec 4, 2021), peaked **#5 Hot 100** (their first top 5 since "Thunder" in 2017), hit **#1 on Radio Songs** (66M weekly audience), 36 weeks on the Hot 100; **54 weeks on Alternative Airplay (9 at #1)** — Billboard ranked it the **14th-most successful song in Alternative Airplay history** (2023). Written with Justin Tranter, produced by Mattman & Robin. [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/harry-styles-as-it-was-tops-hot-100-imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-1235065560/); [Billboard/Rutherford 2023](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/alternative-airplay-chart-35th-anniversary-foo-fighters-all-time-low-rule-1235408126/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy_(Imagine_Dragons_and_JID_song))
- **"Bones"** — Mercury Act 2 lead single; peaked **#47 Hot 100** (2022); their 22nd top-10 on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs (per Reynolds). [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/); [Wikipedia discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons_discography)
- **"Eyes Closed"** — Loom lead single, April 3, 2024. **Did not enter the Hot 100** (peaked #2 on Bubbling Under Hot 100); #13 Hot Rock & Alternative Songs; #89 Canada; syncs: EA Sports NHL 25 soundtrack, WrestleMania XL video package; J Balvin remix May 3, 2024. [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/imagine-dragons-new-song-eyes-closed-1234998617/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_Closed_(Imagine_Dragons_song))
- **"Nice to Meet You"** — May 24, 2024; disco/house-pop; #33 Hot Rock & Alternative, #98 UK (no Hot 100 entry). Produced by Mattman & Robin, mixed by Serban Ghenea. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_(Imagine_Dragons_song))
- **Loom (2024)** — debuted **#22 Billboard 200** (28K units) and **#3 Top Album Sales**; first ID album to miss the top 10 and the first with no Hot 100 single — the streak visibly softened post-2022. Metacritic 67, their first "positive" aggregate score. [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-loom-debuts-top-10-album-sales-chart-1235726970/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loom_(Imagine_Dragons_album))

**Correction to the brief's premise:** "Eyes Closed" is 2024, not 2023 (released April 3, 2024). [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/imagine-dragons-new-song-eyes-closed-1234998617/)

---

## 2) The core repeatable workflow — "build → explosive hook," step by step

This is the documented, repeatable assembly line (confirmed by Reynolds, Alex da Kid, Billboard analysts, and the Hit Songs Deconstructed teardown of "Believer"):

1. **Melodic germ first, theme never.** "I always write the same way: I sit down at a piano, with a guitar or at a computer with no theme in mind and create a soundscape that is an honest output of whatever I'm feeling. I then write lyrics and melody to that feeling. It's been that same way since I was 12." — Reynolds. [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing) His training: "I was a classical pianist for 10 years from six to 16 — playing Chopin, Beethoven and Bach… My brain was formed in that classical piano training and that's still where I write melodies from." [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing)
2. **Stream-of-consciousness hook hunt.** He sings nonsense/stream-of-consciousness over the germ and chases whatever line lands: "A lot of times that's how I'll write lyrics: stream-of-consciousness that comes out and I almost don't even know what I'm saying… If it has meaning, then we'll chase it." (Example: "Gods Don't Pray" began with Reynolds riffing "Gods don't…" — Mattman & Robin flagged it.) [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)
3. **Volume as filter.** With Alex da Kid: "for about eight months we got into a rhythm of writing 2-3 songs a day." [SongwriterUniverse](https://www.songwriteruniverse.com/alex-da-kid-2017/) He claims "I have recorded a song almost every day since then" since age 12. [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/) For every album he arrives with 150–200 demos; for Loom, Mattman & Robin ordered a "wipe the slate clean," and he wrote ~30 songs in 4–6 months in-room with them — the first time he wrote in a room with anyone. [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing); [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)
4. **Beat-first production (Alex da Kid era).** "Radioactive" was "just a beat I made"; "Demons" was "me putting down a track, and the band just writing over it" while "Dan Reynolds was just writing hooks." [American Songwriter](https://americansongwriter.com/songwriter-u-qa-alex-da-kid-discovering-imagine-dragons-crafting-tracks-rihanna-eminem-u2/) The band then layered live drums/guitar/bass over the EDM skeleton — "adding real instrumentation… brought more live emotion to it." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)
5. **The verse → pre-chorus lift → explosive hook architecture.** Billboard's description is the best structural summary: "'Believer' frantically overstuffs its verses before exploding into possibly the year's most cathartic chorus," and "Thunder" builds "a triumphant, brain-burrowing singalong refrain mostly out of a single word." [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/imagine-dragons-biggest-band-2017-interview-8046150/) The Hit Songs Deconstructed analysis adds the mechanics: sequential first-line hooks ("First things first / Second things second…"), and a "C.I.A." (chorus impact accentuator) — a cinematic woosh/lull on the last two beats of the pre-chorus that suspends the lyric ("seein' the beauty through the…") before slamming the chorus ("PAIN!"); plus a mix of sung/shouted/rap-hybrid deliveries per section. [Hit Songs Deconstructed](https://www.hitsongsdeconstructed.com/hsd_wire/believer-blending-in-while-standing-out/)
6. **Minimalism imposed from outside.** The band self-admits overproduction on Smoke + Mirrors ("way over-produced… a huge wall of sound on every song") and hires outside restraint: "Mattman and Robin, that's what they do: very few sounds, but really intelligent and well thought out." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/) On Loom: "They'd say, 'We want it to remain simple and have no fat.'" [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)
7. **Sync-ready dynamics by design.** Trailer/stadium dynamics plus a standing pipeline of placements: "Believer" in a Super Bowl Nintendo Switch ad, "Thunder" in a Microsoft Surface ad (both hit #1 on Billboard & Clio's Top TV Commercials chart), "Whatever It Takes" (WWE/Madden), "Natural" (ESPN college football), "Enemy" (Arcane), "Eyes Closed" (NHL 25, WrestleMania XL). The Guardian's read: "Evolve sounds, almost impressively so, as though it's been created with telly music coordinators in mind." [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/imagine-dragons-biggest-band-2017-interview-8046150/); [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2017/jun/22/imagine-dragons-evolve-review-lifeless-electronic-tinged-arena-rock)

---

## 3) Lyric method — single-word refrains; universal emotional vocabulary; sync-friendly abstraction; occasional biography

- **Single-word / one-phrase refrains.** "Thunder" (Spin counted the word "thunder" ~75 times in the song [Spin](https://www.spin.com/2019/01/imagine-dragons-worst-band-halftime-show/)); "Believer" (the word sung as "PAIN!"); "Natural," "Bones," "Enemy," "Demons," "It's OK." One word = the whole hook; repetition is the hook.
- **Universal pain→empowerment vocabulary.** Reynolds' stated method is writing anthems from bad days: "I write a lot of songs because I'm in a bad place and I'm trying to bring about a false sense of confidence, security and empowerment." [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing) On "Eyes Closed": "That's a song with a lot of false bravado… I'll write a song that is a cup of coffee for me… I love that people hear it and they're like, 'Oh, it's this really confident song.' Because it wasn't really written from a place of that." [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)
- **Metaphor as universalizer.** "When I listen to Night Visions, it's very metaphorical. 'Radioactive' is a song about depression; yet, most people hear it and think it's a song about the apocalypse!" The abstraction is deliberate (grown from writing "mom-proof" lyrics about his Mormon doubts); Rick Rubin pushed him to "peel back a little bit, become more vulnerable." [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing) The trade-off critics name: "Instagram-quote culture" and "tired aphorisms." [Pitchfork (Origins)](https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/imagine-dragons-origins/)
- **Occasional biography, when it charts.** "Wrecked" (sister-in-law's cancer — Pitchfork's rare praise: "touching in its plainspokenness" [Pitchfork (Mercury)](https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/imagine-dragons-mercury-act-1/)); "Bones" — "I was really hyper focused on death… My goal was to write a song about death that was not sad. It's the first time we've ever made a dance song… 'Bones' is supposed to be self-aware and a little bit ironic." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/) "Nice to Meet You" is explicitly autobiographical (dating Minka Kelly — see §6).
- **Self-description of the through-line:** "I write from a very narrative perspective with lyrics and melodies. So it's a very through-line, almost predictable thing to our fans. They know what they're getting. It's not lightning in a bottle. It's just a Dan journal entry with a melody." [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/) Plus the ownership claim: "I've written every single lyric that's ever appeared on any record, and [about] 95 percent of the melodies… It's not a pop machine." [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/imagine-dragons-biggest-band-2017-interview-8046150/)

---

## 4) Topline/singing method — determined-plain belt, pseudo-chants, rhythmic hook

- **The delivery is the hook's engine.** Billboard's Joe Lynch (on why they chart when other rock doesn't): "Their sound deemphasizes guitars. This is not a riff-based rock act, but a beat-based one; couple that with Dan Reynolds' rhythmic, rap-influenced delivery and you have a band uniquely primed for chart/radio success." [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-five-burning-questions-1235050926/) He also lists the "fist-pumping chorus" and "the falsetto" as signature components. [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-five-burning-questions-1235050926/)
- **Registers in opposition.** The vocal scheme is a narrow, exaggerated set: verse = clipped, syllable-dense rhythmic talk-sing; chorus = strained, plain, square-toned belt on repeated title words; plus chant-filler ("woah-ohs" — The Guardian flagged "chart pop's current obligatory chorus of 'woah-ohs'" [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2017/jun/22/imagine-dragons-evolve-review-lifeless-electronic-tinged-arena-rock)). Critics name the same two registers: "knockoff Chris Martin" and "screaming" [Spin](https://www.spin.com/2019/01/imagine-dragons-worst-band-halftime-show/); "Reynolds' snarl-yell, his signature since 'Radioactive,' is one of the most grating sounds in popular music." [Pitchfork (Mercury)](https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/imagine-dragons-mercury-act-1/)
- **The title word is SUNG as a proclamation.** The hook word lands on the highest, longest note of the section, full chest voice, often with a shouted tag ("You made me a, you made me a believer, believer!"; "Thunder, feel the thunder!"). Hit Songs Deconstructed's chart of "Believer" shows the sung→shouted→sung/shouted hybrid mapping section by section — the chorus itself is a shout delivered with melodic pitch, which reads as "anthem" rather than "screamo." [Hit Songs Deconstructed](https://www.hitsongsdeconstructed.com/hsd_wire/believer-blending-in-while-standing-out/)
- **Self-aware plainness.** Reynolds is openly not a "cool" singer — he frames the sound as deliberately unsubtle: "Imagine Dragons is not a subtle band. It's love or hate. It's just Vegas. It's right in your face." [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)

---

## 5) Vocal-anchoring production — the lift, the stomp-clap, the drop

- **Pre-chorus lift is the signature engineering.** The "woosh and lull" spanning the last two beats of the pre-chorus into the first two of the chorus — the C.I.A. — is the single most identifiable device in "Believer," and the same tension-then-catharsis frame repeats across "Natural," "Enemy," "Bones," "Eyes Closed." [Hit Songs Deconstructed](https://www.hitsongsdeconstructed.com/hsd_wire/believer-blending-in-while-standing-out/)
- **Stomp-clap percussion is in the DNA.** The very first hit's beat was a desk: "I wrote 'It's Time' in my dorm room… The stomp clap is me hitting my desk… We added the group's stomps and claps, but we kept the slaps and claps I had done in the dorm room." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/) It remains the live-signature beat of "Radioactive" and the drop sections generally.
- **Music-box / treble piano hooks.** The melodic core is often a thin, high-register piano/synth motif (Thunder's nursery-rhyme riff; the toy-piano hook of "Demons") sitting above a huge low end — "turning down the guitars and turning up every expensive synth pad known to man" per Pitchfork. [Pitchfork (Origins)](https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/imagine-dragons-origins/)
- **Beat-first, drop-based, minimal-instrument chorus.** Joe Lynch: not riff-based but beat-based. [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-five-burning-questions-1235050926/) Mattman & Robin's mandate ("simple and no fat" [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/)) plus Serban Ghenea's mix (Loom and Mercury-era) give the radio sheen; Daniel Platzman described the division of labor: "Songwriting is songwriting… But then we enter the world of production — how are you gonna make that song come to life?" [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/imagine-dragons-biggest-band-2017-interview-8046150/)
- **Home-demo authenticity kept on purpose.** "Thunder" was "recorded at my computer in my front entry room… you can hear a couple of my kids screaming in the background. There was nothing professional about it." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)

## 6) Proof songs (2020–2025)

- **"Enemy" (w/ JID, 2021)** — #5 Hot 100, #1 Radio Songs, 54 weeks Alternative Airplay (9 at #1), ranked 14th-greatest Alternative Airplay song ever. Craft: the whole song existed first ("We had the whole song complete. But we thought it'd be cool to have a guest appearance… I really love JID and suggested him. What he added to it really brought it up a level") — the JID verse itself was years old (started with Mac Miller). Universal-vocabulary mission statement: "'Enemy' is about reconciling internal conflict in a world where it feels impossible to trust even yourself… meant to be both personal and a critique of a society that seems intent on creating division." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy_(Imagine_Dragons_and_JID_song)); [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/harry-styles-as-it-was-tops-hot-100-imagine-dragons-jid-enemy-1235065560/)
- **"Bones" (2022)** — #47 Hot 100; the formula inverted into a four-on-the-floor "dance song about death": "I was really hyper focused on death… My goal was to write a song about death that was not sad… When we play 'Bones' live, everybody's dancing. It's not typical for Imagine Dragons… It's usually more angsty." [GRAMMY.com](https://www.grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-songs-stories-believer-radioactive-thunder-enemy-mercury-act-1-2-new-album-2022-dan-reynolds-interview/)
- **"Eyes Closed" (2024)** — the "false bravado" single: "I could do this with my eyes closed, it's so easy, but the reality is I was not really loving myself or feeling any of those things I was writing about." Did not make the Hot 100 (peaked #2 Bubbling Under) — proof the formula alone no longer guarantees the chart, though it stayed #13 Hot Rock & Alt and picked up NHL 25 + WrestleMania XL syncs. [GRAMMY.com (Loom)](https://grammy.com/news/imagine-dragons-new-album-loom-inspirations-dan-reynolds-writing); [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/imagine-dragons-new-song-eyes-closed-1234998617/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_Closed_(Imagine_Dragons_song))
- **"Nice to Meet You" (2024)** — the biographical variant: written about dating Minka Kelly, whose handclaps are on the record; the "room mic" cheer kept from when they finished the album ("we wanted to add more liveliness… when the second chorus starts, you can hear everybody cheering"). Explicitly anecdotal lyric: "I was buying you those flowers / I was listening for hours / I was shutting up those doubters." Chart reality: no Hot 100 entry (#33 Hot Rock & Alt, #98 UK). [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_to_Meet_You_(Imagine_Dragons_song))

## 8) "The trick" in their words — and the press critique

**The trick (their words):** write every day from feeling, not concept; hunt a one-word chantable hook from stream-of-consciousness; keep the lyric universal ("depression" dressed as apocalypse); let a restrained outside producer strip the track to "no fat"; build verse→pre-chorus-lift→explosive drop; keep dynamics trailer-huge. Reynolds' own summary: "It's not lightning in a bottle. It's just a Dan journal entry with a melody." [Rolling Stone](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/imagine-dragons-dan-reynolds-tabloids-loom-album-1235050767/) Alex da Kid's: write 2–3 songs a day until the hooks accumulate. [SongwriterUniverse](https://www.songwriteruniverse.com/alex-da-kid-2017/) Mattman & Robin's: minimal sounds, maximum polish — the duo described by The Ringer as "pop music as particle physics." [The Ringer](https://theringer.com/2016/3/18/16044232/dark-knights-meet-mattman-robin-pop-music-s-new-hidden-overlords-2524a8727ff0)

**The critique:** the same repeatability is the indictment. Spin: algorithm-bait "motivational platitudes." Pitchfork: "machine learning output" and "low-hanging-fruit music." Guardian: written for TV music coordinators. Classic Rock 2024: "as if selected by algorithms for mass consumption." The band's rebuttal is explicit and consistent: the process predates the algorithm (journal-entry writing since age 12; "I've written every single lyric"), and they absorb the criticism — "very valid. I've got a lot of work to do" — while noting it has real-world cost ("It has added to the depression I've dealt with since youth"). [Stereogum](https://www.stereogum.com/2034084/imagine-dragons-slipknot-nickelback/news/) The honest bottom line: the formula is real, it is documented by both sides, and its effectiveness decayed measurably in 2024 (no Loom single reached the Hot 100), which is itself evidence that the "charts every time" lane depends on radio/sync ecosystem conditions as much as on craft.

## Summary
Imagine Dragons are the last rock act with mainstream Hot 100 muscle: five top-10s ("Radioactive" #2, "Demons" #6, "Believer" #4, "Thunder" #4, "Enemy" #5), the only group in RIAA history with four Diamond-plus singles, and "Radioactive"'s record 87-week Hot 100 run. The repeatable machine is documented in their own words: Dan Reynolds writes alone from a melodic germ and a "false empowerment" lyric — single-word refrains over universal pain/struggle vocabulary — and producer teams (Alex da Kid's beat-first sessions, then the Swedish minimalists Mattman & Robin) build the trademark verse→pre-chorus-lift→explosive-drop hook, engineered for radio and sync. The press critique is equally documented: Pitchfork ("machine learning output"), Spin ("algorithmic playlists"), and Classic Rock ("as if selected by algorithms") all call the formula obvious — yet Billboard staff concede "they've mastered the formula for a hit."
